newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha set for new term, Albania students protest.
newsitem.headline: Berisha set for new term, Albania students protest.

text.p: Albania's ruling Democratic Party selected President Sali Berisha on Thuesday as their candidate in next week's presidential election as students across the Balkan state stepped up protests against the government.
Democratic Party chairman Tritan Shehu said its executive national council voted by 85 votes with five abstentions to back Berisha for a second five-year term.
"He...is the one who has been able to develop democracy and Albania's integration into Euro-Atlantic structures," Shehu told reporters.
Parliament was due to convene later on Thursday to name a date for the parliamentary vote to elect the president, which must be held by March 9.

With the Democrats holding 122 of the 140 seats in the assembly after last year's disputed general election, Berisha was sure to have no trouble winning a fresh mandate and was likely to be unooposed.
The main opposition Socialist Party has refused to take up its seats in parliament after boycotting last May's polls, alleging the Democrats manipulated the vote.

Its leader Fatos Nano, the only serious rival to Berisha, is in jail for corruption. The Socialists say he is being held as a political prisoner and international human rights groups have called for his release.

While the political opposition may feel hamstrung, Berisha and his right-wing party are facing mounting discontent among the people following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes which has left thousands of Europe's poorest citizens out of pocket.

Students were spearheading fresh anti-government protests as violent street clashes abated. In Tirana, around 700 students gathered at a university building to voice support for students on hunger strike in the southern town of Vlore.

Police prevented the Tirana students from entering their building to start their own hunger strike and student leader Premto Gogo was seen being bundled into a car by plain-clothes policemen, one student told reporters.
"The secret police won't allow us to start a hunger strike and they've detained one of our leaders," he said. "But we'll carry on boycotting classes. We're determined to continue the protest."
About 600 students in Gjirokaster, 230 km (145 miles) south of the capital, occupied a nearby lecture hall to protect 46 who went on hunger strike.

Students told reporters that doctors at the town's state hospital had refused to treat them but said one Gjirokaster woman promised to pay for private treatment if necessary as her contribution to the protest.

In Vlore, 140 km (90 miles) south of Tirana, 45 students were still on a hunger strike started last week, while protesters were out on the streets for a 22nd consecutive day in a peaceful demonstration against the investment scandal.
Small rightist opposition parties in parliament have called for a parliamentary debate on the Vlore hunger strike and have declined to put up any candidate for the presidential election.
"There's no point presenting a candidate in a parliament dominated almost 90 percent by the ruling party," Republican Party leader Sabri Godo said.
